As far as I understand (if I'm wrong, someone please correct me):
- The only limitation is the notebook runtime – CPU Notebook ≤ 6 hours, GPU Notebook ≤ 6 hours.
- While playing a level, you can take as many actions as you want.
- If a level has an action limit, the level will restart from zero, and the agent's action count will continue to be summed.
- If the agent completes a level in, say, 1 million actions while a human takes 100 actions, the resulting score for that level will be very small (but still greater than zero).

replies.rawMarkdown:
I see. And do you know the formula is?Edit: On further reading the score for each level is:

 $$\text{score}_{level} = Min\left(1.15, \left(\frac{\text{human turns}}{\text{AI turns}}\right)^2\right)$$

Then the game score (e.g. for 4 levels) is given by:

$$\text{score}_{game} = \frac{1\times S_1 + 2 \times S_2 + 3 \times S_3+ 4\times S_4}{1+2+3+4}$$

I have tested it and you can restart the level as many times as you want (using `env.reset()` ) but all moves are counted included the reset counts as a move.
(Warning: Trying to reset on the first move of a level can reset the game back to the start of level 1!)

replies.rawMarkdown:
Yes, when playing [manually](https://arcprize.org/tasks/ar25), there is a Reset action among the available actions. Pressing it restarts the level from scratch. How this works for an agent — I haven't studied yet.
The calculation method is described [here](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/data):
>For each level completed, the agent's action count is compared to a human baseline (first-time test-testers).
Per-level score = min(human_actions / agent_actions, 1.0), then squared (a raw score of 0.5 becomes 0.25).
Per-game score = Weighted average of level scores (weighted by level index, 1-indexed).
Total score = Average of all individual game scores.
Final output is a score between 0%–100%.

comments.rawMarkdown: How I'm interpreting it, is that there is a human baseline score. Every time you move, or make an action, except scanning the board, which a human would do through vision. Those 100 actions of sorts, retries, resets, bumping into a wall or any action. All those count against your score. The setup prevents brute force attempts. If your app beats the human score, they cap you at 115%. Every action you take that's more than a human starts to deplete your score and is weighted. That's why we see scores like .66%. They could have completed every level of each game 6/6, but still had to many attempts for it to matter. So if you try to brute force the answer, your percentage drops unless you solve in fewer turns than a human. That took me a while to figure out. That's my take, which has me up at night, and making me hope I'm not chasing another Collatz conjecture.

replies.rawMarkdown:
My understanding from looking at the code is  that a reset at the start of a level causes the scorecard to create a new run. The action counts for this run are 0, but the scoring code sums across all runs. Hence, there is no way to nullify any actions previously taken. This applies to the public scoring code. The gateway, or any other entity that generates the LB/PB scores, may or may not use the came code.

On a related note, a manual reset makes sense in some cases, because it provides a shorter path to the end solution. A simple example would be a situation in which we need to move an obstacle out of the way but previous moves made it impossible. Rather than waste actions until the level resets itself, we can reset it ourselves and save those actions.
